summary:
Côte d'Ivoire does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices states that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground. The sources assembled here do not cover entry, visa or identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers.

Non-state violence against LGBTQ people is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report records three deaths within the community during that year. Police responses to violence committed by non-state actors were described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often blaming the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Peer-reviewed research on Ivoirian travestis reports harsher stigmatisation and violence than is experienced by sexual minorities whose gender presentation avoids drawing attention.
tangentialFactors:
A UNDP report of December 2024, marking ten years of African Commission Resolution 275 on protection of LGBT+ people, includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space and inclusion. The country-level findings of that overview are not reproduced in the material available here.

A New York Times article of October 2024 on the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire exists but could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so none of its content informs this record.

The US State Department's 2011 human rights report for Côte d'Ivoire supplies a general baseline rather than trans-specific findings: it covers the post-electoral crisis, in which some 3,000 people died alongside widespread sexual violence and displacement. Its LGBT-specific content is limited.

Comparative framing from the academic literature is that gender normativity functions as protection in Côte d'Ivoire: sexual minorities who conform to expected gender presentation attract less hostility than those who do not.
localsOnly:
Travestis in Côte d'Ivoire, defined in the literature as people born anatomically male who live as women, face harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity keeps them out of view. Domestic rights groups have distanced themselves from travestis, leaving that population underserved by Ivoirian advocacy organisations.

Research published in Critical African Studies in 2015 by Thomann and Corey-Boulet documents the violence and social exclusion experienced by travestis alongside their resilience, and examines the isolation they faced after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Handling of complaints by the authorities was reported as somewhat better than in previous years, a change that accrues to residents as well as visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or identity-document screening rules for transgender travellers to Côte d'Ivoire, including whether gender markers on foreign passports attract scrutiny at border control.

Unresolved: Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire. Where trans detainees are placed (birth sex versus identity), whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any listed publication; on the HRW country page, 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link.

Unresolved: the Côte d'Ivoire country overview in the UNDP report of December 2024 was not read into this record, so its assessments of prosecution rates, access to justice and civic space remain unverified here.

Unresolved: the New York Times article of October 2024 could not be retrieved (HTTP 403) and contributes no findings.
